name: Court de Gébelin's Tarot — The Birth of the 'Book of Thoth' (1781)
description:
# Court de Gébelin's Plates (1781)

## At a glance

The hinge of the whole story. In 1781 the Protestant scholar **Antoine Court de Gébelin**
published an essay declaring the Tarot de Marseille a survival of the ancient Egyptian
**Book of Thoth**. He offered **no evidence** — and was wrong — but he converted a card
game into a "sacred text" and launched two centuries of occult tarot. Bundled with his
essay was a second piece by the **Comte de Mellet**, which first proposed *reading the
cards* and linking them to the Hebrew alphabet.

## Origin & dating

Published in volume 8 of de Gébelin's encyclopedic *Le Monde Primitif* (1781). The story
runs that he saw the tarot game being played in a Paris salon (Mme Helvétius's) and
"recognised" Egyptian allegory in the trumps. His redrawn plates "corrected" the
Marseille images toward what he imagined Egyptian originals looked like.

## Provenance & evidence

The text and plates survive and are public-domain. What does **not** exist is any
evidentiary basis: this predates Champollion's decipherment of hieroglyphs (1822), so
de Gébelin's "Egyptian" reading was pure imagination projected onto Italian Christian
imagery.

## Game or divination?

This is the **birth of the divinatory/occult claim** — but as *theory*, not practice.
De Gébelin allegorised; it was the Comte de Mellet (and then Etteilla) who turned the
idea into a method. The grammar should treat de Gébelin as the **origin of the myth**,
explicitly dated 1781, and never as evidence about the decks' actual 15th-century origin.

## The fear question

**No fear at all — the opposite.** De Gébelin published openly, under his name, in a
respectable subscription encyclopedia read by the Parisian elite (Franklin was a
subscriber). Far from hiding "occult" knowledge, he *announced* it as prestigious
ancient wisdom. The 18th-century salon treated this as fashionable erudition, not
dangerous magic. The occult overlay was, at its birth, a **public, high-status
intellectual fad**.

## Counter-voices

This file is where the "suppressed occult history" claim must be weighed most carefully.
De Gébelin is the *source* of the Egyptian-origin belief that many practitioners still
hold. Defenders argue he intuited a real esoteric substrate. The scholarly verdict
(Decker, Depaulis, Dummett) is firm: the Egyptian genealogy is **invented**, not
recovered — a Romantic-Enlightenment fantasy about Egypt, not a transmission from it.
Importantly, debunking de Gébelin does **not** debunk the *real* later history of
divinatory practice or its persecuted practitioners; it only removes a false pedigree.

## Open questions / corrections owed

- Clearly separate de Gébelin's essay from Mellet's appended essay — they differ (e.g.
  trump-to-Hebrew-letter assignments).
- The plates are interpretive redraws; flag them as such, not as historical decks.

## Sources & further reading

- "Antoine Court de Gébelin," Wikipedia; "De Gébelin's Tarot Essay in Le Monde Primitif,"
  Mary K. Greer.
- Decker, Depaulis & Dummett, *A Wicked Pack of Cards* (1996).

**RESEARCH NOTE (2026-06-13).** Two etymologies are often blurred: the **'Royal Road' (Tar + Ro)** is **Gébelin's**; the **'Ta-Rosh = road/science of Thoth'** is the **Comte de Mellet's**. Gébelin's birth year is contested across sources (1719/1724/1725/1728). The Wheel's Sphinx/Typhon/Hermanubis figures are later Lévi/Waite additions, NOT in Gébelin's 1781 plate. See [research/decks/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/decks/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md).

## One source per deck

This deck carries **Court de Gébelin's** 1781 reading and nothing else. **Papus's** *Le
Tarot des Bohémiens* (1889), which used to sit on every card here, is now its own deck —
`papus-tarot-des-bohemiens`.

sections.Iconography: A traveller in motley with a staff and bundle, a beast at his leg — the Marseille Fool, copied into the plate.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

One cannot mistake the Fool in this card — his bauble, his harlequin coat hung with shells and bells: he walks very fast, as a madman does, carrying his little bundle behind him, imagining he can thus escape the Tiger that bites at his haunches. As for the bag, it is the emblem of his faults that he would not see; and that Tiger, the emblem of his remorse which follows galloping behind and leaps up in his saddle.

This beautiful idea, which Horace framed so well in verse, was not his — the Egyptians had not overlooked it: it was a commonplace, taken from nature ever true. We call this card Zero, though it is placed in play after XXI, because it counts for nothing when alone and has value only as it gives value to others — precisely like our zero — showing thus that nothing exists without its folly.
sections.Tradition Note: Court de Gébelin's claim (1781) that the tarot is an ancient Egyptian 'Book of Thoth' is a myth — the tarot is a 15th-century Italian card game. But this essay INVENTED esoteric tarot: every occult deck and the whole practice of tarot divination descend from this single, mistaken, fertile idea.
sections.Research note:
**What changed (vs. its parent):** Same image; the change is conceptual — the Marseille's nameless wandering jester is fixed as **"zero,"** the head of an alphabet-of-22, giving the Fool the structural prominence every later occult deck grants it [@web_trionfi_gebelin]. 

*Sources:* [@trionfi], [@web_robertplace_firstoccult], [@web_tarotforum_mellet], [@web_trionfi_gebelin].

*Full card-by-card research:* [research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md).
sections.Scene: A figure in a jester's costume walks with a bundle on a stick, a small animal at his heels. The plate is an engraving based on a Marseille-type deck, rendered in de Gébelin's archaeological style.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin identified this card with Typhon or the god of chaos in his Egyptian reading of the tarot.

sections.Iconography: A figure at a table of cups, coins and knives, wand raised.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

The first of all the trumps — going upward, or the last going downward — is a Cup-and-Ball Player; one recognises him by his table covered with dice, cups, knives, balls and so forth, by his Jacob's staff or Mage's wand, and by the ball he holds between two fingers and is about to conjure away.

He is called Bateleur in the card-makers' designation — the common name for persons in that trade. Is it necessary to say that the word comes from baylê, a stick?

Placed at the head of all the estates, he indicates that the whole of life is but a dream, a sleight-of-hand; that it is like a perpetual play of chance or the collision of a thousand circumstances that never depended on us, on which every general administration necessarily exercises a powerful influence.

But between the Fool and the Juggler, is Man not well represented?

sections.Research note:
**What changed (vs. its parent):** The Marseille's street-performer *bateleur* is elevated from fairground conjuror to a quasi-priestly figure of cosmic agency, his cups/coins/swords/baton turned into element-symbols — the first step of the long transformation of this card into the occult "Magician" [@web_robertplace_firstoccult]. 

*Sources:* [@web_robertplace_firstoccult], [@web_villarevak_gebelin].

*Full card-by-card research:* [research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md).
sections.Scene: A standing figure at a table spread with various small objects and tools. He wears a wide-brimmed hat and gestures with a wand. The engraving simplifies the Marseille Bateleur.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin called this card the 'Juggler,' the first principle of magic and skill in the Egyptian Book of Thoth narrative.

sections.Iconography: A veiled, enthroned woman in a tiara with a book.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Numbers II and III represent two women; numbers IV and V, their husbands: these are the temporal and spiritual heads of Society. The second card is the female spiritual head — the Grand Priestess, or the female Pope, adorned with the papal tiara and seated on a throne. We know that among the Egyptians women played a large role in sacred matters, and that they had their own priestesses. She holds on her knees an open book in which she reads.

The divination that the High Priestess inspires relates to things of the spirit, religion, and the inner life — all that belongs to the domain of faith and contemplation rather than action.

But this essay INVENTED esoteric tarot: every occult deck and the whole practice of tarot divination descend from this single, mistaken, fertile idea.
sections.Research note:
**What changed (vs. its parent):** The Marseille *Papesse* — an awkward Christian image (a female pope) often explained away as Pope Joan or a heresy — is re-titled and re-sexed into **Egyptian priestess-goddess**, removing the Christian embarrassment and making the card the keystone of the Isis reading [@web_traditionaltarot_isis]. 

*Sources:* [@web_robertplace_firstoccult], [@web_traditionaltarot_isis].

*Full card-by-card research:* [research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md).
sections.Scene: A seated woman in a veil and headdress, holding a book. She wears a papal tiara, shown enthroned frontally. The plate follows the Marseille Papesse closely.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin identified her as Isis, the keeper of sacred knowledge, rather than a Christian Papess.

sections.Iconography: A crowned woman with sceptre and eagle shield.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Number III represents the Queen — the Empress. She and the Emperor (IV) share the same attributes: the eagle in a shield, and the sceptre surmounted by a globe crowned with a cross, called Tau, the sign par excellence. Together they are the temporal sovereigns of human society, governing the visible world through power and law.

The Empress in particular governs fertility, the abundant powers of the natural world, and the generative forces through which the temporal order renews itself from one generation to the next.

sections.Research note:
**What changed (vs. its parent):** Modest — the feudal Empress is folded into the Egyptian royal frame as Osiris's counterpart; the change is the *context* (Egyptian sovereignty) rather than the image (confidence: medium — Gébelin's text is least explicit here). 

*Sources:* [@web_robertplace_firstoccult], [@web_traditionaltarot_isis].

sections.Scene: A winged empress is shown seated on a throne, holding a sceptre, with an eagle-bearing shield at her side. Her crown and wings appear in the engraved version.
sections.Symbol: Identified by de Gébelin as Isis in her role as queen of heaven and guardian of the natural world.

sections.Iconography: A bearded sovereign in profile with sceptre and shield.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Number IV is the King — the Emperor. He and the Empress bear the eagle and the tau-sceptre as their shared marks of temporal sovereignty. Gébelin groups the four great figures (II, III, IV, V) together as the four heads of human society: the King and Queen govern temporal life; the Pope and Priestess govern spiritual life.

The Emperor represents the rational organizing force of governance — the principle of law, hierarchy, and measured authority that maintains order across time.

**What changed (vs. its parent):** The Holy Roman Emperor becomes an **Egyptian** king-god (Osiris), anchoring the Isis/Osiris/Typhon family Gébelin scatters across the trumps [@web_traditionaltarot_isis]. 

*Sources:* [@web_robertplace_firstoccult], [@web_traditionaltarot_isis].

sections.Scene: A crowned emperor sits on a throne in profile, holding a sceptre and orb. The plate renders the standard Marseille Emperor in engraved line.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin identified this figure with Osiris, king of Egypt and lord of the living.

sections.Iconography: A tiara'd pontiff blessing two acolytes.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Number V is the male spiritual head — the Jupiter or Grand Hierophant of the Egyptians, which our card-makers have called the Pope. He is shown enthroned, his triple crown upon his head, his hand raised in blessing, two worshippers before him. His authority is of the spirit, complementing the temporal authority of the Emperor (IV).

Gébelin sees in him the personification of the transmitted sacred knowledge of Egypt — the initiated priest who stands between the divine order and the human community, translating cosmic law into teachable doctrine.

**What changed (vs. its parent):** The Catholic Pope is de-Christianised into the **pagan high priest of the mysteries**, exactly paralleling the Papess→Isis-priestess move; this is where the modern title "Hierophant" originates [@web_robertplace_firstoccult]. 

*Sources:* [@web_robertplace_firstoccult], [@web_villarevak_gebelin].

sections.Scene: A hierophant or pope is enthroned between two pillars, raising his hand in blessing toward two kneeling figures. He wears a triple crown and holds a triple cross.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin associated this card with the Egyptian high priest, the intermediary between gods and humanity.

sections.Iconography: A youth between two women beneath a winged Cupid drawing his bow.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

The card represents Marriage — the union of two figures beneath the figure of the Divine Genius, or Love, who hovers above them with drawn bow. Gébelin interprets this as the sacred Egyptian institution of marriage, presented as the fundamental bond of social life from which all else follows.

Above the couple, the winged Genius with his arrow represents the cosmic force of attraction that draws like to like — not sentimental love but the constitutive principle of human union. Between the Fool who wanders alone and the married pair who form the fundamental cell of society, the whole arc of social life is already contained.

But this essay INVENTED esoteric tarot: every occult deck and the whole practice of tarot divination descend from this single, mistaken, fertile idea.
sections.Research note:
**What changed (vs. its parent):** The Marseille's love-triangle-under-Cupid is first narrowed to **"Marriage"** (Gébelin), then moralised into the **Choice / Vice-and-Virtue** allegory (Mellet) that later cartomancers inherited — though the earliest cards show simple love, not moral choice [@web_benebell_lovers]. *Correction to existing grammar: the Vice/Virtue–Hercules reading is Mellet's, not Gébelin's.*. 

*Sources:* [@web_benebell_lovers], [@web_robertplace_firstoccult].

*Full card-by-card research:* [research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md).
sections.Scene: A young man stands between two women while a winged Cupid aims an arrow from above. The engraving follows the Marseille 'Amoureux' composition.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin called this card the 'Marriage' of Osiris and Isis, or the union of opposing principles.

sections.Iconography: A crowned prince in a canopied chariot drawn by two horses.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

The Chariot shows a conqueror, a warrior king, erect in his war-chariot drawn by two horses. In the Egyptian system this figure represents Osiris triumphant — the principle of solar victory over darkness, of civilization over chaos, of the ordered cosmos over the formless void.

Gébelin sees the two horses — one looking forward, one aside — as the dual nature of temporal power: the horse of force and the horse of intelligence, which must be driven in concert if victory is to be sustained. The canopy above the charioteer indicates that his power is not merely military but cosmic, sheltered by the dome of heaven itself.

But this essay INVENTED esoteric tarot: every occult deck and the whole practice of tarot divination descend from this single, mistaken, fertile idea.
sections.Research note:
**What changed (vs. its parent):** The generic Renaissance triumph-chariot is given an **Egyptian royal/Osirian** gloss; image unchanged, frame Egyptianised (confidence: medium on the explicit "Osiris" label for this specific card). 

*Sources:* [@web_robertplace_firstoccult], [@web_villarevak_gebelin].

*Full card-by-card research:* [research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md).
sections.Scene: A crowned warrior in a canopied chariot is drawn by two horses. He holds a sceptre. The Marseille chariot composition is reproduced faithfully in the engraving.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin identified this as Osiris triumphant, returning victorious from a military campaign.

sections.Iconography: An enthroned woman with sword and balance.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Justice sits enthroned with sword and scales. Gébelin identifies her as one of the four Cardinal Virtues that the Egyptian system placed among the twenty-two trumps — the others being Prudence (XII), Strength (XI), and Temperance (XIV).

He interprets Justice as the foundational principle of all ordered society: without the impartial weighing of actions and consequences, no community can sustain itself. The Egyptians, he argues, placed this principle among the highest social goods because they understood that cosmic order (Ma'at) and social justice were one and the same principle operating at different scales.

But this essay INVENTED esoteric tarot: every occult deck and the whole practice of tarot divination descend from this single, mistaken, fertile idea.
sections.Research note:
**What changed (vs. its parent):** Little visual change; Gébelin gathers Justice (VIII), Strength (XI), Temperance (XIIII) and the re-read Hanged Man as Prudence (XII) into the **complete set of four cardinal Virtues**, presenting their presence as proof of a designed wisdom-system [@web_benebell_lovers]. 

*Sources:* [@web_benebell_lovers], [@web_robertplace_firstoccult].

*Full card-by-card research:* [research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md).
sections.Scene: A crowned woman sits on a throne holding a sword upright and scales in the other hand, in the standard Marseille Justice pose.
sections.Symbol: Justice identified with Ma'at, the Egyptian goddess of truth, balance, and cosmic order.

sections.Iconography: A cloaked old man with a staff and a shielded lantern.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

The Hermit represents the Sage — the wiseman who carries his lantern to light the way for others. Gébelin interprets him as the Egyptian philosopher-priest, the keeper of sacred knowledge who does not display it in palaces but carries it through the world, available to whoever is willing to seek it out.

The staff on which he leans is his staff of experience; the lantern he raises illuminates not the horizon but the ground immediately before the seeker. This is the mode of transmission of the ancient wisdom: not proclamation but availability — the sage does not come to you; you must seek him out.

But this essay INVENTED esoteric tarot: every occult deck and the whole practice of tarot divination descend from this single, mistaken, fertile idea.

**What changed (vs. its parent):** The Marseille's *Hermite* (sometimes read as Father Time / Old Age) is recast as the **searching philosopher (Diogenes)** — a wisdom-seeker rather than a figure of mortality [@web_robertplace_firstoccult]. 

*Sources:* [@web_robertplace_firstoccult].

sections.Symbol: De Gébelin interpreted this card as the 'Sage' — the Egyptian philosopher who carries the lamp of wisdom through darkness.

items.name: 10 — Wheel of Fortune (La Roue de Fortune)

illustrations.scene: Wheel of Fortune (La Roue de Fortune)

sections.Iconography: A wheel turned by figures rising and falling.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

The Wheel of Fortune belongs to the cosmological section of the Tarot — cards representing the great physical and temporal forces that govern human life from above. Gébelin reads it as the Egyptian image of Fate or Providence: the wheel that turns, raising some and lowering others, subject to a cosmic law that no individual can reverse.

The figures on the wheel — human or animal — represent the great estates of humanity in their cyclical turns: what is high will descend; what is low will rise. Only the sphinx at the summit, the enigma of wisdom, remains unmoved by the wheel's turning — the sage who understands the law is not thrown by its application.
sections.Tradition Note: Court de Gébelin's claim (1781) that the tarot is an ancient Egyptian 'Book of Thoth' is a myth — the tarot is a 15th-century Italian card game. But this essay INVENTED esoteric tarot: every occult deck and the whole practice of tarot divination descend from this single, mistaken, fertile idea.
sections.Research note:
**What changed (vs. its parent):** Essentially unchanged in meaning; **note for accuracy** — the later Sphinx-couchant / Typhon-descending / Hermanubis-rising figures belong to **Lévi and Waite's** reconstructions, **not** Gébelin's plate, which keeps the Marseille's nondescript beasts. Do not import them into the 1781 reading [@web_benebell_lovers]. 

*Sources:* [@web_benebell_lovers], [@web_robertplace_firstoccult], [@web_villarevak_gebelin].

*Full card-by-card research:* [research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md).
sections.Scene: A spoked wheel at the card's centre turns while figures cling to its rim at various positions. A sphinx or animal figure sits atop the wheel.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin associated the Wheel with the Egyptian cycle of the Nile flood — the year's turning and the alternation of abundance and scarcity.

sections.Iconography: A woman calmly parting a lion's jaws.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Strength is one of the four Cardinal Virtues — the one that Gébelin specifically identifies with the Egyptian principle of mastery over the animal nature. A woman opens or closes a lion's mouth: the image of the human spirit (feminine, in the Egyptian tradition, because the spirit is the receptive principle that draws the divine into matter) mastering the vital force without weapons.

Gébelin sees this as a key Egyptian teaching: the highest form of strength is not military force but the capacity to transform the energies of life — including our own animality — rather than suppress or destroy them. The lion does not die; it is befriended.
sections.Tradition Note: Court de Gébelin's claim (1781) that the tarot is an ancient Egyptian 'Book of Thoth' is a myth — the tarot is a 15th-century Italian card game. But this essay INVENTED esoteric tarot: every occult deck and the whole practice of tarot divination descend from this single, mistaken, fertile idea.
sections.Research note:
**What changed (vs. its parent):** Image and meaning essentially as in the Marseille; the change is its enrolment in Gébelin's four-Virtues scheme [@web_benebell_lovers]. 

*Sources:* [@web_benebell_lovers], [@web_robertplace_firstoccult].

*Full card-by-card research:* [research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md](https://github.com/PlayfulProcess/recursive-tarot/blob/main/research/cards/court-de-gebelin-tarot.md).
sections.Scene: A woman gently holds open the jaws of a lion. The standard Marseille Strength composition is reproduced in the engraving.
sections.Symbol: Physical force tamed by moral virtue; de Gébelin read this as the Egyptian virtue of courage.

sections.Iconography: A youth suspended by one foot from a frame.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Prudence — which Gébelin calls the fourth Cardinal Virtue in the Tarot (Arcanum XII) — is shown as the Hanged Man. The identification is startling, but Gébelin argues that for the Egyptians, true prudence required the capacity to see the world from the inverse perspective: to hang oneself, so to speak, between the normal and the inverted view, and to choose action only after having considered all perspectives including the uncomfortable and the counter-intuitive.

The voluntary suspension of the Hanged Man is thus not punishment but the posture of the prudent person who refuses to act from the first impression and insists on testing every assumption by turning it upside down.

sections.Scene: A man hangs inverted by one ankle from a gallows, his free leg crossed behind, his arms relaxed at his sides.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin erroneously interpreted this card as the 'Prudent Man,' suggesting a figure in contemplation rather than punishment or sacrifice.

sections.Iconography: A skeleton with a scythe among the fallen — the card left unnamed in the Marseille.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Death — the unnumbered card — shows a skeleton with a scythe harvesting a field in which crowned heads, severed hands and feet emerge from the ground. Gébelin notes that the card carries no number precisely because Death belongs to no category and no rank: it is the great equalizer that the Egyptians placed among the trumps as the unavoidable force that stands outside all social hierarchy.

His reading is not gloomy: death, for the Egyptians, was the moment of transition, the passage to the next life. The scythe that cuts also prepares the ground for new growth — an agricultural metaphor entirely in keeping with the Egyptian civilization's dependence on the Nile flood that destroys in order to fertilize.

sections.Symbol: De Gébelin saw this as Typhon, the Egyptian destroyer, moving through creation with no regard for rank.

sections.Iconography: A winged figure pouring liquid between two vessels.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Temperance is the fourth of the Cardinal Virtues in the Tarot — an angel or winged figure pouring liquid between two vessels. Gébelin reads this as the Egyptian principle of right mixture, the art of maintaining dynamic equilibrium between opposing forces.

He connects it to the figure of Isis mixing and preparing the sacred substances — a reading that makes Temperance less a moral virtue than a cosmological skill: the capacity to hold opposites in productive relationship without allowing either to dominate or destroy the other. This is the art of the priest, the physician, and the alchemist.

sections.Symbol: De Gébelin identified this as Temperance in the Pythagorean sense: harmony and measured proportion.

sections.Iconography: A horned, winged figure over two bound captives.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

The Devil is Typhon — the Egyptian principle of darkness, chaos and destructive inversion. Gébelin sees him as the necessary counterpart of the divine order: where Osiris represents the light of ordered civilization, Typhon represents the forces of chaos, dissolution and inversion that are always threatening to overwhelm it.

The figures chained to the pedestal are those whom Typhon has claimed — who have given themselves over to the inverted order. The card is not primarily moral but cosmological: it represents the Egyptian understanding that the cosmos is a battleground between order and chaos, and that the outcome of that battle depends on the choices made by conscious beings.

sections.Symbol: De Gébelin associated this card with Typhon-Set, the Egyptian embodiment of chaos and the principle of destruction.

sections.Iconography: Figures fall from a tower struck by fire from the sky.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

The Lightning-struck Tower — what Gébelin calls the House of God or the Maison-Dieu — represents the destruction of the Tower of Babel, or more generally the overthrow of human presumption by divine power. The stone tower, struck by a bolt from heaven and losing its crown, represents any human institution that has overreached its proper limit and attracted the corrective lightning of cosmic law.

For Gébelin this is not catastrophe but justice: the gods do not permit human constructions — physical, social, or intellectual — to usurp the place of the divine order. The card is a warning, not a prophecy: those who build within the proper measure will not attract the lightning.

sections.Iconography: A naked woman kneels pouring two urns into water and onto land, beneath a great star and seven small ones.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Gébelin groups cards XIX (The Sun), XVIII (The Moon), and XVII (The Star) together as the three great luminaries — the physical lights that the Egyptians placed in the cosmological section of the Tarot. The Star shows the eight-pointed star of the Egyptians — the star of Isis, the star of navigation and of hope — surrounded by seven smaller stars, with a kneeling woman below pouring the waters of life.

The Star is the celestial lamp that guides the traveller and the mariner through the night. Gébelin reads it as the Egyptian image of divine providence made visible: the star that never sets, that promises arrival after the long journey.

sections.Scene: A kneeling figure pours water from two pitchers near a pool. Above, a large star is flanked by seven smaller stars.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin identified this card with the heliacal rising of Sirius (the Dog Star), which heralded the Nile flood and the new year in Egypt.

sections.Iconography: A dripping moon over two dogs and a crayfish between two towers.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

The Moon is the second of the three luminaries — the card of night, of the tidal forces that govern all liquid matter, of the dream-world and the subterranean. Gébelin reads it as the Egyptian card of the moon-goddess, the keeper of the night mysteries, the measurer of time through cycles.

The towers on either side of the lunar landscape are the pylons of an Egyptian temple, the ritual gateway between the human and the divine world. The crayfish or scarab emerging from the water represents the primitive life-force that the moon draws upward from the depths — the lunar tides of psychic matter that no solar light can reach.

sections.Symbol: De Gébelin saw this as the Moon in its Egyptian role as timekeeper, marking the month and guiding nocturnal navigation.

sections.Iconography: A radiant sun over two children by a wall.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

The Sun is the first of the three luminaries and the most powerful — the card of Ra, of Osiris, of the solar force that generates life on earth. Gébelin reads the image of two children dancing beneath a radiant sun as the Egyptian symbol of the twin principles of nature — passive and active, night and day, moon and sun — united under the beneficent governance of the solar light.

The enclosure below — the low wall of the garden — represents the civilized earth, the tilled and cultivated domain of human life, warmed equally by the sun's impartial generosity. No figure in the Tarot receives the solar light more fully than these two children at play.

sections.Iconography: An angel trumpets while the dead rise from a tomb.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

The Last Judgement shows the Egyptian scene of resurrection — the moment when the dead are called forth from their tombs by the angel's trumpet. Gébelin reads it as the Egyptian belief in the resurrection of Osiris and its extension to the human soul: after death and the weighing of the heart, the justified soul rises and is restored to life in a transfigured form.

The angel above is Thoth or Hermes — the divine messenger who stands at the boundary between the living and the dead, who calls the deceased to their hearing before Osiris and announces the verdict of the scales. This card represents the belief that all actions are ultimately weighed, and that consciousness does not end at death.

sections.Iconography: A dancing figure in a wreath, the four beasts in the corners.
sections.Court de Gébelin's Egyptian Reading:
[Translated from Court de Gébelin's *Du Jeu des Tarots*, Monde Primitif vol. VIII, 1781]

Gébelin begins his reading of the entire Tarot with this card — it is the card with which he made his initial discovery. The World shows a woman at the centre of an oval wreath, dancing; in the four corners stand the four living creatures of the Egyptian cosmology — Man, Eagle, Lion and Bull — the four pillars of the universe.

This is, he writes, the card that "showed me the allegory" in a single glance, during that game of Tarot with friends that launched his investigation. He read it as the image of Time surrounding the World — the oval wreath being the year, the four creatures being the four seasons or the four cardinal points, and the dancing figure within being the earth or the soul of the world, animated and free within the eternal cycle.

items.name: The 'Book of Thoth' — The Birth of Occult Tarot

sections.What happened here: In 1781 Antoine Court de Gébelin looked at an ordinary Tarot de Marseille — a card game — and declared it the last survivor of an ancient Egyptian 'Book of Thoth', a hieroglyphic encyclopaedia of priestly wisdom carried west by the 'Gypsies'. He was wrong on every count: tarot is a 15th-century Italian game, the 'Egyptian' reading is invented, and the Romani have no link to Egypt. Hieroglyphs would not be deciphered for another 40 years.
sections.Why it matters: And yet this single essay created esoteric tarot. Within a decade Etteilla built the first divination deck on it; Lévi added the Kabbalah; Wirth, the Golden Dawn, Waite, and Crowley followed. Every occult tarot — and the whole idea that tarot tells fortunes — descends from this beautiful mistake. The companion essay by the Comte de Mellet, in the same volume, first proposed the Hebrew-letter associations and the reverse-order Egyptian cosmogony.
sections.Scene: The 22 atout plates from Antoine Court de Gébelin's 'Le Monde Primitif' (1781), Volume VIII. Each plate is a rough line engraving based on a Tarot de Marseille deck, accompanied in the text by de Gébelin's elaborate theory that the tarot is the surviving fragments of the Egyptian Book of Thoth.
sections.Symbol: De Gébelin's plates inaugurated the occult tarot tradition. His Egyptian identification — later refuted by Egyptology — proved enormously influential, launching two centuries of esoteric tarot commentary. The plates themselves are historically important as the first published scholarly reproduction of tarot cards.
